draft.title: Writing your own narrative
card: Start with a clear idea you want the story to carry, such as the cost of silence or the pull of home. Every choice should serve that idea.
Narrator
decide who tells the story. A first-person narrator is close to events but sees only part of them. A third-person narrator can stand back.
Structure
decide the order of events. You might go in time order, or open near the end and move back to show how it happened.
Central image
choose one image to return to, such as a locked gate. Its meaning can shift as the story goes on.
draft.remember: Pick an idea first, then choose a narrator, structure and image that carry it.

a.q: Maya wants her story to show how silence can grow between two sisters. Which choice best suits that idea as a central image?
opts: A phone that is left unanswered on a table
A large crowd cheering at a football match
A list of the sisters' favourite foods
A map of the town where they live
a.why: An unanswered phone stands for silence and distance, so it carries her idea. A map or a list is a detail that does not point to the idea.

b.q: Leo wants readers to feel a narrator's guilt about an old mistake. Which narrator choice suits this best?
opts: A first-person narrator looking back on what he did
A narrator who describes only the weather
A third-person narrator who never mentions thoughts
A narrator who has no link to the events
b.why: A first-person narrator looking back lets the reader hear guilt in his own voice. The other choices hide the character's feelings, so guilt would be harder to show.
b.clue: Which voice is closest to the narrator's feelings?

a.best: A phone that is left unanswered on a table

b.best: A first-person narrator looking back on what he did

problems.detail: The distractors (favourite foods, a football crowd, a town map) plainly have nothing to do with silence, so the question is too easy for Year 11 Advanced and does not test how an image carries an idea.

Distractors such as a narrator who describes only the weather or has no link to the events are implausible, so the question is too easy for Year 11. A stronger distractor, such as a close third-person narrator, would test real understanding.

check.summary: Both questions are accurate and match the card and the writers' answers, but their distractors are so implausible that the questions are too easy for Year 11 Advanced.

proposal.title: Writing your own narrative
card: Start with a clear idea you want the story to carry, such as the cost of silence or the pull of home. Every choice should serve that idea.
Narrator
decide who tells the story. A first-person narrator says I and tells events in their own voice. A close third-person narrator says he or she and follows one character's thoughts from outside.
Structure
decide the order of events. Time order keeps readers waiting to learn what happens. Opening near the end shows the outcome first, so the story asks how and why.
Central image
choose one image to return to, such as a locked gate. It shows the idea rather than stating it, and its meaning can shift each time it appears.
proposal.remember: Pick an idea first, then choose a narrator, structure and image that carry it.

a.q: Maya wants her story to show silence slowly growing between two sisters. Which plan uses a central image best?
opts: A phone that rings less each time it appears
A phone call described once in the opening scene
A new object linked to silence in each scene
A line where the narrator says they grew apart
a.why: A phone that rings less each time is one image that returns and shifts, so it shows the silence growing. A phone call described once is tempting because it links to silence, but it never returns, so it cannot track the change.
a.clue: A central image is one image the story keeps coming back to.

b.q: Leo wants readers to hear a man's guilt in his own voice and to know from the first page that his mistake happened. Which plan fits?
opts: First person, opening near the end then moving back
Close third person, opening near the end then moving back
First person, told in time order from the beginning
Close third person, told in time order from the beginning
b.why: Only a first-person narrator speaks in his own voice, and opening near the end shows the outcome first. Close third person is tempting because it follows the man's thoughts, but it says he, so readers hear the guilt from outside rather than in his own words.
b.clue: Check both parts: whose voice, and when readers learn the outcome.

why: the fresh check found a problem

a.best: A phone that rings less each time it appears

b.best: First person, opening near the end then moving back

problems.detail: The card says a close third-person narrator 'follows one character's thoughts from outside'. Close third person gives readers access to a character's inner thoughts and often echoes their voice, so 'from outside' is confusing. It could teach students that close third cannot get inside a character's mind. Something like 'follows one character closely, sharing their thoughts while still saying he or she' would be clearer.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match the card. The only problem is that the card describes close third person as following thoughts 'from outside', which is misleading and should be reworded.

It could teach students that close third cannot get inside a character's mind. Something like 'follows one character closely, sharing their thoughts while still saying he or she' would be clearer.
